The Arithmetic of a Falling Number: Root Cause Analysis at Depth

Exp40 reading page. Working systematically from a metric change to an actionable cause — the identity that always holds, the inference that never comes free, and the places where competent practitioners honestly disagree.

1. Two rooms, two falling numbers

At 07:40 on Monday, 4 May 2026, Nandita Rau, Vice-President of Product at Suljhan Systems in Pune, was looking at a contractual number. Suljhan sells a claims-adjudication platform to seven Indian health insurers; its headline operating metric is the straight-through processing rate, the share of submitted claims the rules engine settles with no human touch. Across February the blended STP rate had sat at 57.3%. In the week ending 1 May it was 46.6%. Two of Suljhan's master service agreements carry an STP floor of 52% with service credits below it, and the largest of those clients — whose chief operating officer had asked for a written explanation by 15 May — was also the one whose renewal, worth about ₹41 crore over three years, went to committee in July. Weekly claim volume over the same period had risen from 1.42 lakh to 1.86 lakh. Nandita's engineering director had a theory ready before the meeting began: the new outpatient product launched in March was "just harder to adjudicate". It was a comfortable story. It was also, as the arithmetic would show within three days, almost exactly backwards.

Eleven days later and 840 kilometres south, Imran Qureshi, Head of Product at Silsila Labs in Bengaluru, faced a softer-edged version of the same problem. Silsila's consumer app answers questions about documents a household already owns — an insurance policy, an electricity bill, a school circular — in nine Indian languages. Its quality metric is the answer-accept rate: the share of answers a user neither retries, rephrases, nor marks down within the session. It had run at 74.0% through April. On 18 May it was 65.0%. Four things had changed inside those eleven days: the underlying model vendor shipped a version upgrade on 6 May, the retrieval index was rebuilt on 9 May, Tamil and Marathi launched on 4 May, and the offline evaluation judge — itself a model — was upgraded on 7 May. Imran's investors' update was due on 29 May, and the sentence he could not yet write was the only one that mattered: whether the product had got worse, or had merely been asked harder questions by more people.

Both are root cause analyses. Only one of them has a root cause in the sense the phrase implies.

2. The idea, and who disputes it

Root cause analysis of a metric change is the practice of moving from an observed movement in an aggregate to a statement of the form this specific, verifiable condition changed, and here is the share of the movement it accounts for. It rests on one piece of arithmetic that is always true and one piece of inference that never is. The arithmetic: any weighted-average metric is exhaustively decomposable into the rates of its parts and the weights of its parts, so every movement can be attributed, without residue, to changes in rates, changes in mix, or the interaction of the two. The inference: that the slice where a movement concentrates is the thing that caused it. Nothing in the arithmetic licenses that step, and the discipline's entire intellectual history is a record of people discovering this the expensive way.

The practice has four distinct ancestries, and much of today's disagreement is unrecognised inheritance. From industrial quality control came Walter Shewhart's control charts in the 1920s and W. Edwards Deming's separation of common-cause variation, which is the system behaving normally, from special-cause variation, which is something new. Deming's central and still under-absorbed warning was that intervening on common-cause variation — investigating and adjusting in response to ordinary noise — measurably increases the variance of the system. He demonstrated it with a funnel and marbles. From Toyota's production system came the Five Whys and, through Kaoru Ishikawa, the cause-and-effect diagram: the insistence that a nameable, correctable condition sits under a recurring defect. From demography came the piece most product managers have never heard of and use every day: Evelyn Kitagawa's 1955 standardisation method for separating rate change from composition change in mortality statistics, rediscovered in labour economics as the Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition and rediscovered again, nameless, in every growth team that has ever said "it's a mix shift". And from statistics came the counterfactual tradition — Rubin's potential outcomes, Pearl's causal graphs, and the applied machinery of difference-in-differences and synthetic control — which holds that a cause is a claim about what would have happened otherwise, and that no amount of slicing produces one.

Four schools argue, and it is worth being precise about the proposition each would and would not sign.

The decomposition school, the analytics mainstream, would sign: every aggregate change is fully attributable to segment rates and segment weights, and finding the concentration is most of the work. It would not sign: the concentrated segment is the cause. The counterfactual school would sign: a cause is only established against a comparison unit that did not receive the change. It would not sign: a well-reconciled decomposition establishes anything causal. The systems-reliability school — Deming's descendants by way of modern incident practice, Sidney Dekker and John Allspaw among them — would sign: outcomes emerge from many interacting conditions, so the useful output of an investigation is the control you add, not the culprit you name. It would not sign: this one thing caused it. The base-rate pragmatists, who run the operations of large consumer businesses, would sign: most metric movements are instrumentation, seasonality, mix, or a known release, in that order, and the ordering of hypotheses matters more than the depth of any one of them. They would not sign: you must explain the whole gap. These are not four ways of saying the same thing. They produce different first moves, different stopping rules, and different answers.

3. Mechanics, worked

Begin with the identity, because it does the heavy lifting and because most teams use a degraded version of it. Let a metric M be a weighted average over segments i, with weights wi (each segment's share of the denominator) and rates ri. Then the change between a baseline period 0 and a current period 1 splits into exactly three terms:

ΔM = Σ wi0(ri1 − ri0)  +  Σ (wi1 − wi0)ri0  +  Σ (wi1 − wi0)(ri1 − ri0)

The first term is the within or rate effect: what the change would have been had the mix stayed frozen. The second is the between or mix effect: what it would have been had every rate stayed frozen. The third is the interaction, and it is the term teams drop. Dropping it is usually harmless when segments move a point or two; it is catastrophic when a segment's share and its rate move sharply at the same time, which is precisely the situation that produces the most alarming dashboards. Read the table against the story Nandita walked in with. Outpatient volume grew from 30% to 44% of claims, which is exactly what the "harder mix" narrative pointed at — and mix, computed properly, contributed plus 1.1 points. The outpatient family had always adjudicated above the blended average. The 10.7-point fall is a rate collapse inside one segment, from 66% to 40%, plus an interaction term that exists only because that segment was growing while it broke. A team that had run the two-term version of the decomposition, folding the interaction into whichever bucket was convenient, would have reported either a 11.8-point rate problem or a 2.5-point mix problem, and would have argued about which for a week.

Decomposition is recursive, and the next cut is where the analysis stopped being arithmetic and started being useful. Splitting outpatient by plan variant: legacy OPD, 39% of outpatient volume, adjudicating at 68% — unchanged since January. The new OPD Plus variant, launched 9 March, 61% of outpatient volume, adjudicating at 22%. Check the reconciliation: 0.39 × 0.68 + 0.61 × 0.22 = 0.399, against an observed 40%. The residual is a tenth of a point. That is the signature of a complete decomposition, and it is what licenses the next question rather than answering it: what is true of OPD Plus claims that is not true of legacy OPD claims? The answer, found by pulling eighty rejected OPD Plus claims and reading them, was that the variant requires a diagnostic-report attachment which the rules engine had no parser for, so every such claim fell through to manual review by design. Nobody had shipped a bug. A product launch on one side of a contract had silently redefined the workload on the other.

Three steps sit implicitly around this arithmetic, and experts do all three before touching a segment. The first is diff the change log, not the funnel: list every dated change in the window — deploys, config flags, pricing, partner launches, regulatory circulars, logging changes — before forming a hypothesis, because the cheapest explanation for a step function is something that stepped. The second is establish the noise floor. For a rate metric, the standard error of a segment's rate is approximately the square root of p(1−p)/n. Suljhan's pre-authorisation family, at 18,600 claims a week and a 45% rate, has a standard error of 0.36 points, so its one-point improvement is real but trivial. A single hospital chain inside that family, at 420 claims a week, has a standard error of 2.4 points — a five-point swing there is indistinguishable from nothing. The third is count your tests. Suljhan's dashboard offers seven dimensions averaging nine values each: sixty-three cells. Viewed daily across a ten-day investigation, that is 630 comparisons, and at a conventional five-percent threshold roughly thirty-one of them will look anomalous with nothing whatsoever wrong. This is why the most exciting cell on a segmentation dashboard is usually the smallest one, and why it is usually noise.

4. When the method applies, and when it misleads

Five conditions can be stated as testable claims. One: the metric is a weighted average whose weights and rates are both observable. Suljhan passes cleanly; claim family is a recorded field. Silsila passes only nominally, because "intent" is assigned by a classifier, which means the weights themselves are model output and can drift when the classifier is retrained — a decomposition can produce a spurious mix effect that is really a labelling change. Two: the movement is large relative to the noise floor of the smallest segment you intend to trust. Suljhan's 10.7 points against a 0.4-point standard error is not in doubt; Silsila's nine points are also safe, but its per-intent cuts at a few thousand sessions are near the edge, and its rerun variance — the same 500 prompts scored twice against the same model gave results 1.8 points apart — means an AI product's noise floor exceeds the binomial estimate. Three: the dimension along which the world actually changed is one you can slice by. This is the condition that fails silently and most expensively. Four: the causal structure is roughly stable within the window. Silsila fails this outright: four changes in eleven days, mutually confounded by calendar. Five: someone would act differently depending on the answer.

The method is actively misleading in four situations. When the variation is common-cause, investigating it does not merely waste effort — the resulting adjustments increase variance, which is Deming's point and remains the most-ignored finding in the field. When the metric is a ratio whose denominator is endogenous to the change, the movement can be entirely an artefact of who is being counted: a filter that removes low-intent traffic raises conversion while improving nothing. When the output will be used to assign blame, the investigation stops producing information, because people who control the change log learn to annotate it less. And when the movement is a slow composition trend, there is no event to find; the honest answer is "the business is becoming a different business", which is a strategy conversation wearing an analytics costume.

5. Hard edges

In multi-product companies the first failure is ownership: the blended metric belongs to a committee, each segment belongs to a team, and no one owns the mix. Suljhan's STP rate is contractual at the blended level but engineered at the segment level, which is how a client's product launch became Suljhan's SLA breach with no defect on either side. In two-sided marketplaces the decomposition must run on both sides on different clocks, because supply churn shows up in a demand metric with a lag set by how long the marketplace's memory is. In regulated settings a circular carries a date, which is analytically a gift — an exogenous step you did not choose — but privacy rules often forbid retaining the fields you would most want to segment on, so the regulated analyst works with deliberately coarse dimensions and must reason about what a missing cut could hide. In hardware-plus-software the killing problem is that rollouts are sequenced by physical batch, so firmware version, manufacturing lot, installation vintage and service contractor are all nearly collinear with each other and with the calendar; telemetry also arrives with a lag measured in weeks, so the window you are analysing is not the window that has finished. In AI-native products the stack has four independent change cadences — input distribution, retrieval layer, model version, and the evaluation judge — each capable of moving a quality metric, three of them invisible in a product change log, and one of them capable of moving the measurement while the product stands still.

At the organisational seams, what mature companies say and what they do diverge. They say they run blameless five-whys reviews. What the good ones actually run is an annotation layer: a single timestamped ledger into which marketing, data engineering, platform, finance and partner teams write every dated change, queryable alongside the metric. The ledger is unglamorous, politically contested — it makes every team's deploy cadence visible — and it collapses the median investigation from nine days to two, because the first move stops being "let me segment" and becomes "what changed on the eleventh".

6. What separates an expert

They check the denominator before the numerator.

The tell is a rate that moved while the count behind it did not. When a conversion rate falls and the absolute number of conversions is flat, nothing has got worse; the population being counted has changed. Experts reflexively plot numerator and denominator as separate series before they look at the ratio, because a ratio hides which of two numbers moved and roughly half of all "metric drops" are denominator events — a bot filter switched on, a new low-intent acquisition channel, a session definition changed from thirty minutes to sixty. The obvious reading, that the product got worse, is wrong because the product was never measured against a constant population.

They know that mix and rate can have opposite signs.

The tell is an aggregate that moved further than any individual segment. If no segment fell by ten points but the blend fell by ten, the blend is being driven by weights, not rates — and the converse, Suljhan's case, is that a mix story can be confidently told about a movement mix actually opposed. The obvious reading — the growing segment is the weak segment, so growth caused the fall — is wrong whenever the growing segment's baseline rate was above the blended average, which is surprisingly often, because segments grow when they are working.

They treat Simpson's paradox as a diagnostic, not a curiosity.

The tell is every segment improving while the total declines. Practitioners who have met this once stop asking "did it get better or worse" and start asking "for whom, and how many of them are there", because the paradox is not an anomaly but the ordinary consequence of unequal weights. Its real information content is about the business: it says the composition of demand is changing faster than product quality is, which is a commercial finding dressed as a statistical one.

They read the shape before they cut the data.

The tell is a practitioner who opens the daily series at full resolution rather than the weekly roll-up. A step, a ramp, a sawtooth and a dip-with-recovery each have disjoint cause families, so thirty seconds with the raw series eliminates three-quarters of the hypothesis space. The obvious approach, going straight to the segmentation dashboard, is wrong because segmentation is expensive in attention and the shape is free.

They know rolling windows smear steps into ramps.

The tell is a decline whose slope is suspiciously constant over exactly twenty-eight days. A step change in the underlying behaviour, viewed through a twenty-eight-day rolling metric, appears as a linear ramp lasting precisely the window length and then flattening. Teams routinely hunt for a gradual cause for what was a single-day event, or worse, watch a ramp continue for four weeks and escalate repeatedly while nothing new is happening. The diagnostic is to recompute the metric on non-overlapping daily or weekly buckets.

They expect the cause to be measurement more often than they would like.

The tell is a break that lands on a deploy date but affects segments that the deploy did not touch. Instrumentation changes — an event renamed, an SDK upgraded, a consent banner altering what fires, a de-duplication rule added — are the single largest category of metric movements in most consumer products, and they are the last hypothesis teams reach because no one's roadmap contains them and no one is proud of them. The obvious reading, that a behaviour changed, is wrong because the behaviour was never observed directly; only its log was.

They track the fraction explained, and they know when to stop.

The tell is a practitioner who says "this accounts for about eighty per cent of the gap" unprompted. A story that reconciles to seventy per cent is not seventy per cent right; it may be a correct account of one cause sitting on top of an undiscovered second. But the mirror-image error is chasing a residual already inside the noise floor. Experts compute both the explained fraction and the floor, and stop when the unexplained part is smaller than the smallest thing they could detect.

They distrust the smallest cell on the dashboard.

The tell is excitement about a segment nobody had named before. Automated multi-dimensional attribution tools reliably surface narrow, exotic cells, because the search rewards explanatory power per unit of volume and small cells have extreme rates by construction. The correct response is to ask how many cells were searched and what the expected count of spurious findings is at that threshold — and then to pre-register the two or three dimensions that theory says matter, and look there first.

They separate the cause from the countermeasure.

The tell is an investigation that ends with a mechanism and a decision presented as one sentence. Suljhan's mechanism — a missing parser — admits at least four responses: build the parser, change the contract's measurement basis, price the variant differently, or refuse the workload. Root cause analysis is silent between them. Practitioners who conflate the two smuggle a business judgement into an analytical deliverable, where it is harder to contest because it arrives wearing the authority of the arithmetic.

They know that finding a cause is not the same as being able to act on it.

The tell is a clean, confirmed, entirely external cause: a competitor's promotion, a monsoon, an exam calendar. Novices treat this as failure, because nothing is fixable; experts treat it as the most valuable outcome available, because it converts an open-ended investigation into a forecasting input and stops the organisation from shipping a reactive change to a problem that will resolve itself.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

The arithmetic is identical everywhere; what changes is sample size, the availability of a counterfactual, and who controls the dimensions. In consumer products, volume permits three-way segmentation with trustworthy rates, and the binding constraint is multiplicity — too many cells, too much noise-chasing. In B2B and enterprise, a metric movement often traces to fewer than twenty accounts, so root cause work becomes account review and structured conversation; a segment of three accounts cannot support a significance test, and pretending otherwise is the characteristic enterprise-analytics error. The compensating advantage is that enterprise causes are knowable by asking: someone at the client can simply tell you their plan launched on 9 March. In platforms and marketplaces the decomposition must be two-sided and lagged, and the metric that falls is usually not the metric that broke. In hardware, collinearity by manufacturing batch is the dominant hazard and staged rollouts should be randomised within batch rather than sequenced by it, which converts every routine rollout into a free experiment. In AI products, the stack's four clocks confound each other, the input distribution is non-stationary by design, and the measurement instrument can itself be a model that changed.

Stage matters less than people claim. The honest difference is that a seed-stage company with 4,000 weekly sessions has no statistical power at all and should do root cause analysis by watching twelve session recordings and calling five customers, which is not a lesser method but a different one with better resolution and worse coverage. A late-stage company has power and tooling, and its characteristic failure is the opposite: it can only segment along dimensions someone thought to instrument, so its blind spots are structural rather than statistical. What does not differ by stage, contrary to the usual telling, is the discipline of reconciliation — the small company that skips it wastes a week it cannot afford.

8. Three worked cases

Kadiyaan Freight: every lane improved, the number fell

Kadiyaan operates a road-freight marketplace matching shippers to truck operators. Its core metric is load fill rate, the share of posted loads matched within six hours. Between August and September it fell from 81.0% to 77.7%. The decomposition, on two lanes, is stark: short-haul (under 400 km) held 55% of loads at a 90% fill rate and became 35% of loads at a 91% fill rate; long-haul held 45% at 70% and became 65% at 70.5%. Both lanes improved. Check the blend: 0.35 × 0.91 + 0.65 × 0.705 = 0.777. The mix effect is −4.1 points, the rate effect is +0.7, interaction +0.1. Matching had got better and the business had got worse, because short-haul shippers — the segment Kadiyaan served best — were leaving for a competitor. The actionable metric was never fill rate; it was posted-load volume by lane, which no one had put on the dashboard because it is an input, not an outcome.

Silsila Labs: three suspects innocent, one guilty, and a moving ruler

Imran's decomposition by intent produced a rate effect of −3.75 points, a mix effect of −4.22 and an interaction of −1.08, summing to the observed −9.0. The mix term was the new-language launch: Tamil and Marathi users skewed hard toward compute-and-compare questions ("is this bill higher than last month") and away from simple lookups, moving lookup's share from 41% to 29%. That is not a quality regression; it is a harder question mix, and it accounts for nearly half the fall. But inside compute-and-compare the rate itself fell from 58% to 44%, and that was real. Replaying 1,200 archived compute-and-compare queries against each combination — old model with old index, new model with old index, new model with new index — isolated it to the index rebuild, which had re-chunked table-heavy PDFs so that a bill's current-month and previous-month columns landed in different retrieved passages. The model upgrade was innocent. The judge upgrade was worse than innocent: it had moved the offline evaluation score by four points in the opposite direction, which is why the offline dashboard said quality had improved while users said it had not, and why the team lost its first four days arguing about which dashboard to believe.

Soothra Instruments: a rigorous analysis that was wrong

Soothra places connected point-of-care haematology analysers in roughly 2,300 clinics. Its service metric is uptime-in-window: the share of devices completing at least one valid run per working day. It fell from 94.1% in February to 88.6% in April. The analysis looked exemplary. Devices on firmware 4.2 ran at 86.9%; devices still on 4.1 ran at 94.0%; the gap reconciled the aggregate to within half a point. Soothra rolled 700 devices back to 4.1 over three weeks. Their uptime rose to 88.2% — not 94%. The rollback, which the team had intended as a fix, functioned accidentally as the experiment nobody had run. Firmware 4.2 had been pushed by installation batch, newest devices first, and those devices carried a reagent-cartridge optical sensor from a second supplier qualified in December: 91% of 4.2 devices had the new sensor against 6% of 4.1 devices. Version and sensor lot were almost perfectly collinear, and no dimension in the analytics warehouse recorded sensor lot at all — condition three had failed silently. The cost was seven weeks, about ₹3.4 crore in service credits, and one lost hospital-group tender. The recovery mattered more than the diagnosis: Soothra built a per-device change ledger covering firmware, supplier lot, reagent formulation and service contractor; adopted a standing rule that no single-dimension attribution is accepted until tested against an orthogonal dimension; and began randomising rollouts within batch rather than sequencing by it. Uptime returned to 93.6% by July, but the durable asset was the ledger.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Stopping at the first plausible story. Early warning: the explanation arrives before the reconciliation. Diagnostic question: what percentage of the gap does this account for, computed? Cost of catching it late: an engineering quarter spent on an innocent subsystem, as Suljhan's team nearly spent on outpatient rules complexity in general rather than one plan variant in particular.

Confounded rollouts. Early warning: the treatment group was selected by time, geography or batch rather than at random. Diagnostic question: what else is nearly perfectly correlated with this dimension? Cost late: Soothra's seven weeks and ₹3.4 crore.

Segment hunting. Early warning: the finding is a cell nobody had heard of, with a large effect and a small n. Diagnostic question: how many cells did we look at, and how many would look this extreme by chance? Cost late: a reorganisation of the roadmap around a random fluctuation, and the loss of the team's credibility when it reverts.

Measurement change mistaken for behaviour change. Early warning: the break is a clean step on a date with no product deploy, or it appears in segments the deploy did not touch. Diagnostic question: has the event definition, the SDK, the filter or the denominator changed? Cost late: a genuine product change reverted on the evidence of a broken ruler.

Investigating common-cause variation. Early warning: the movement is inside two standard errors, and this is the third such investigation this quarter. Diagnostic question: what is the week-to-week standard deviation of this metric when nothing is happening? Cost late: not merely wasted analyst time but a measurably noisier product, as the organisation adjusts in response to noise.

Blame contamination. Early warning: the change log becomes less detailed over successive quarters, and teams begin announcing changes after they land. Diagnostic question: in the last three investigations, did the output name a team or name a control? Cost late: the ledger dies, and every future investigation reverts to nine days of guessing.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether a root cause exists. The systems-reliability position holds that complex socio-technical outcomes have contributing conditions, not causes, and that naming one is a narrative convenience that stops learning early; its evidence is the incident literature, where post-hoc single causes routinely fail to prevent recurrence. The opposing position, held by most operators of large digital products, is that this is true of catastrophes and false of metric movements: the empirical base rate is that a step change in a product metric is explained by one dated change perhaps three times in four, and the systems view, applied to routine work, produces expensive investigations that end in philosophy. For the systems view to be wrong about metrics, single-cause explanations would have to hold up under subsequent testing most of the time, which in software they largely do; for the operator view to be wrong, the recurrence rate after single-cause fixes would have to be high, which in hardware and in safety-critical systems it is.

Whether decomposition without a counterfactual is worth anything. The counterfactual school points at Soothra: a perfectly reconciled attribution that was simply false, and could only be corrected by an accidental experiment. The decomposition school answers that the identity is not offered as causal evidence at all; it is a search-space reduction that makes a cheap confirmatory test possible, and demanding a control group before any narrowing is a counsel of paralysis in a business with a ten-day clock. The disagreement is real and is about sequencing. It would be settled against the decomposition school if narrowed hypotheses failed confirmatory testing at rates near chance; the available evidence, thin and mostly internal to firms, suggests they do much better than chance and much worse than practitioners assume.

How much of the gap must be explained. One camp requires reconciliation to within the noise floor, arguing that unexplained residual is where the second, worse problem hides — Silsila's real regression was hiding underneath a mix story that explained half the movement. The other camp argues that the marginal value of explained variance falls sharply, that investigations have real cost, and that a team which insists on full reconciliation for every wobble will simply stop investigating anything. Both are describing real organisations. The reconciling position — stop when the residual is below what you could act on — is easy to state and, in practice, nobody agrees on what "act on" means.

Who should run the analysis. The team that shipped the change has the context and the change log and moves three times faster; it also has a motive, and the literature on motivated reasoning is not kind. An independent analytics function is slower and frequently misidentifies causes because it does not know what was deployed. Firms split roughly evenly, and the split does not correlate with sophistication. What the better firms on both sides share is not the org chart but the ledger: when every change is timestamped by its own author before anyone knows a metric moved, the incentive problem shrinks considerably.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four visible ways. They ask what the metric's normal variation is before asking why it moved, and they sometimes conclude that the correct action is none. They insist on the order — confirm, diff the change log, decompose, reconcile, then test — and they notice immediately when a colleague has jumped to segmentation without a change log, because that is the move that costs a week. They report a number with its explained fraction and its residual attached, the way an engineer reports a measurement with a tolerance, and they are visibly uncomfortable presenting a story that reconciles to two-thirds. And they hold the cause and the decision apart in public: having established that a missing parser cost eleven points, they say so, and then say separately that whether to build the parser is a commercial judgement they do not own. The person who has merely studied the topic produces a well-segmented deck that concludes with a recommendation and no residual.

12. What the two decided

Nandita wrote to the client's chief operating officer on 13 May with three statements and one request. The blended STP rate fell because one plan variant, launched by the client on 9 March, requires an attachment the rules engine cannot parse, and that variant alone accounts for 10.6 of the 10.7 points. Mix is not the cause; had OPD Plus adjudicated at legacy OPD's rate, the blend would have stood at 57.9%, above February. Suljhan will ship the parser within two sprints. The request was the interesting one: that the SLA be restated per plan variant rather than blended, since a contractual commitment on a blended rate gives one party a metric the other party can move unilaterally by launching a product. The renewal committee accepted the parser; the contract change went to a longer negotiation, which is the honest outcome.

Imran did three things and refused a fourth. He rolled back the table-chunking change for document types with tabular layouts, recovering about five of the nine points within a week. He instituted a constant-composition accept rate — the same metric reweighted to April's fixed intent-and-language mix — reported alongside the raw figure, so that future launches cannot masquerade as quality regressions or conceal them. He separated the offline judge score from the production behavioural metric in all reporting, and required that any judge upgrade be run in parallel with the old judge for two weeks. What he refused was to revert the model upgrade, which three people had wanted on day two and which the replay showed was innocent. In his investor note he wrote that the product's quality had fallen by 3.8 points and its audience had got harder by 4.2, and that only the first was his to fix.

Discussion questions

1. Suljhan's contract specifies a blended metric that the client can move by changing its own product mix. Is the correct remedy analytical (report per-variant rates), contractual (restate the SLA), or commercial (price the variant)? Who should decide, and what does the root cause analysis contribute to that choice beyond the number?

2. Soothra's rollback was intended as a remedy and functioned as an experiment. Under what conditions should a team deliberately roll back to half the affected population rather than all of it, and what would that have cost Soothra had the firmware genuinely been the cause?

3. Imran reported a decline in quality and a hardening of the audience as two separate numbers. A board member argues this is evasion: users experience one number, and it went down. What is the strongest form of that objection, and what would you have to believe about the purpose of a metric to accept it?

13. Going deeper

  1. Segmenting users in analytics — the dimensions you can cut by determine which causes are findable at all; Soothra's failure was a segmentation failure before it was an inference failure.
  2. Guardrail metrics — guardrails are frequently what moved, and a guardrail and a primary metric moving together usually points to one shared upstream change rather than two problems.
  3. Signal vs noise; product vs measurement — the two questions that must be answered before any investigation begins, and the two most often skipped.
  4. The data review for leadership — where a reconciled story with a stated residual is worth more than a confident one, and how to present a decomposition without smuggling in a decision.

The Ten-Day Window: Root Cause Analysis at Mashaal Grocers

A reading page on working systematically from a metric drop to an actionable cause.

1. The scene

On the morning of Monday, 3 March 2025, Devika Iyer, Group Product Manager for Growth at Mashaal Grocers, opened the weekly metrics deck and found the number she had been dreading. Checkout conversion — the share of sessions that added an item to cart and went on to place a confirmed order — had fallen from a steady 71% through early January to 64% by the last week of February. Weekly sessions had actually grown, from roughly 500,000 to 520,000, so the absolute count of lost orders was larger than the percentage drop suggested: about 36,000 fewer confirmed orders in a single week than the January run rate would have predicted. Mashaal's board was due to meet on 13 March to approve capital for twelve new dark stores in Tier-2 cities, a bet that depended on the unit economics holding at something close to the current conversion rate. If Devika walked in with "conversion is down and we don't know why," the expansion would likely be shelved for a quarter. If she walked in with the wrong explanation and the board acted on it — say, killing a discount programme that was innocent, or approving expansion into a market that was quietly broken — the cost of being wrong confidently would be worse than the cost of admitting uncertainty. She had ten days. Her task was not to guess at a story that fit the number, but to do root cause analysis properly: find out, with evidence, which part of the business had actually changed.

2. The idea

Root cause analysis, or RCA, is the disciplined practice of tracing an observed change in an outcome metric back to the specific, verifiable condition that produced it, by successively decomposing and segmenting the metric until the change stops looking uniform and starts looking concentrated. It was invented to solve a narrow but recurring problem: an aggregate number moves, everyone in the room has an opinion about why, and without a method the loudest or most recent hypothesis wins the meeting regardless of whether it is true. The discipline has its roots in industrial quality control — Kaoru Ishikawa's cause-and-effect diagrams at Kawasaki in the 1960s, and Toyota's "Five Whys" practice on the production line, both built to stop factory teams from patching symptoms while the actual defect kept recurring. Digital product teams inherited the same logic and applied it to funnels, cohorts, and segments instead of assembly lines. The sentence Devika could say in the boardroom without sounding glib is this: before we decide what to fix, we cut the metric until the drop disappears into a segment small enough to explain with evidence. RCA does not itself prove causation; it narrows an intractably vague question — "why did conversion fall?" — into a tractable one: which 15% of sessions accounts for nearly all of the fall, and what is true about them that was not true in January?

3. How it actually works

The mechanics run in a fixed order, and the steps practitioners most often skip are the first and the last. Step one is to confirm the drop is real: rule out a measurement artefact by checking that the event-logging pipeline, the date-range definition, and the denominator (sessions with at least one add-to-cart) have not silently changed, and that the drop survives a like-for-like comparison against the same weekday mix and time zone. Step two is to decompose the metric into its structural components — here, sessions to add-to-cart, and add-to-cart to confirmed order — because a drop in a blended metric can originate anywhere along that chain, and treating "conversion" as one indivisible number hides which stage actually broke. Step three is to segment each component along the dimensions that plausibly differ: city tier, device, new versus returning customer, payment method, delivery slot. Step four is the step most teams rush: check whether the drop is uniform across every segment (which points to a systemic cause, such as a platform-wide outage or a pricing change applied everywhere) or concentrated in one segment (which points to something specific to that slice of the business). Step five generates hypotheses from wherever the concentration lands, rather than from whatever anecdote reached the team first. Step six checks whether the guardrail metrics — refund rate, cart-abandonment complaints, app-crash rate — moved at the same time, since a metric and its guardrail moving together often signals one shared upstream cause rather than two separate problems. Step seven, the one teams skip most often, is arithmetic reconciliation: do the segment-level changes, weighted by their share of volume, actually add up to the aggregate change observed, or is there a residual left over that the leading hypothesis does not explain? Only once that residual is small does RCA hand off to a controlled comparison or a genuine experiment to confirm the mechanism, because segmentation alone establishes correlation between a segment and a drop, never proof that the segment's defining trait caused it.

4. The worked example

Devika's team pulled the funnel for the last week of January against the last week of February. In January: 500,000 sessions, 300,000 reached add-to-cart (a 60% rate), and 213,000 of those became confirmed orders — 71% of add-to-cart, the number on the dashboard. In February: 520,000 sessions, 305,000 add-to-cart (58.7%, essentially flat), but only 195,200 confirmed orders, a checkout-stage rate of 64%. The drop lived almost entirely in the second stage: cart-to-order, not session-to-cart. That ruled out a top-of-funnel story — a marketing-channel change, say — and pointed the team at checkout itself.

Segmenting the checkout stage by city tier told the real story: two things had changed at once, Tier-2's own conversion rate was low, and Tier-2's share of total volume had grown sharply.

The second pass tested an alternative the team had floated: that a payment-gateway change in mid-February had hurt Tier-1 too, masking a smaller decline behind its reported 72%. Substituting a hypothetical Tier-1 rate of 68% into the same equation gives (0.68 × 220,000 + 0.43 × 85,000) ÷ 305,000 = 0.610 — a 61% aggregate, three points below what was actually observed. Since the real aggregate was 64%, the data rule out a meaningful Tier-1 decline: had Tier-1 truly fallen that far, the blended number would have been worse than it was. That single check killed a plausible hypothesis before it consumed a week of the payments team's time.

5. The nuances to hold onto

Mix shift versus rate change

The distinction between a segment's own rate changing and a segment's share of volume changing is the single most common source of RCA errors, precisely because both produce the same symptom in the aggregate. Mashaal's case was almost pure mix shift; a team that skipped the reweighting step would have concluded Tier-2 checkout was "broken" and rushed a fix, when the more accurate statement is that Tier-2 has always converted at roughly this rate and the business is simply doing more of it.

Concentration is not causation

Finding that the drop concentrates in Tier-2 narrows the search; it does not identify the mechanism. Tier-2 could convert worse because of unfamiliar UI, thinner catalogue depth, slower delivery promises, or a demographic with less card penetration. Segmentation tells you where to look, not what you will find.

Reconciliation, not vibes

A hypothesis should account for close to 100% of the observed gap once volumes are weighted correctly. A team that stops at "Tier-2 converts worse" without checking whether that fact alone reconciles the aggregate risks leaving a second, unrelated cause undiscovered underneath a story that only explains part of the number.

Guardrails as clues, not verdicts

A guardrail metric moving in the same window as the primary metric is a clue about shared upstream cause, not proof of one. Mashaal's refund rate had ticked up slightly in February; that made a payments or fulfilment problem worth checking, but the guardrail's movement had to be reconciled by segment exactly as the primary metric was, since a guardrail can also mix-shift for reasons unrelated to the metric under investigation.

Granularity has a floor

Cutting by city tier, then by device, then by delivery slot, then by hour of day quickly produces segments of a few hundred sessions where random noise looks like a pattern. RCA should stop segmenting a dimension once the segment sizes are too small to distinguish a real rate difference from sampling variation, which for a metric like checkout conversion usually means keeping segments above a few thousand sessions per week.

Cross-sectional snapshots can hide cohort maturation

Comparing this week's Tier-2 conversion to this week's Tier-1 conversion treats Tier-2 as a fixed population, but many of those users are in their first or second week ever on the app. A cohort view — tracking a specific signup week's conversion as it ages — can show whether Tier-2 users converge toward Tier-1 rates by week four, which would mean the problem is onboarding friction that resolves itself, not a permanent ceiling.

RCA narrows hypotheses; it does not confirm mechanism

Even a clean, fully reconciled segmentation only tells you where the change is concentrated and rules out where it is not. Confirming that a specific mechanism — say, thin Tier-2 catalogue depth — actually causes lower conversion still requires either a controlled test (adding SKUs to a subset of Tier-2 stores and comparing) or a natural experiment, because two markets can differ on a dozen dimensions at once.

RCA cannot tell you what to do

Even a fully confirmed cause is silent on the decision. Knowing that Tier-2 converts worse because of catalogue depth does not by itself say whether Mashaal should slow expansion, subsidise inventory, or accept the lower rate as the cost of growth; that judgment belongs to the people who own the trade-off, informed by, but not dictated by, the analysis.

6. How this differs by business type and stage

In a high-volume consumer app like Mashaal's, RCA leans on statistical segmentation because sample sizes are large enough to slice by city, device, and cohort simultaneously and still trust the rates. In B2B products, the same discipline is applied with far smaller populations — sometimes a metric drop traces back to fewer than twenty accounts — so root cause work often becomes account-by-account review and structured win-loss interviews rather than statistical cuts, because a segment of three enterprise accounts is not a segment a significance test can speak to. In marketplaces, RCA has to look on both sides of the transaction: a demand-side metric like checkout conversion can fall not because buyers changed but because supply thinned, as happened partially in Mashaal's own case with Tier-2 stock levels, so a one-sided funnel view risks missing the actual lever entirely. Stage matters too: an early-stage company with a few thousand weekly sessions rarely has enough volume for clean statistical segmentation and instead relies on direct user interviews and session recordings to build the same picture qualitatively, while a large company can lean on automated anomaly detection and pre-built segment dashboards — with the opposite risk, that the dashboard only surfaces the dimensions someone thought to configure in advance, and the true cause sits along a dimension nobody built a filter for.

7. Common mistakes

Fixing the first segment found. The symptom is a team that identifies a low-converting segment and immediately proposes a fix, without checking whether that segment's own rate actually changed or whether its growing share of volume is doing all the work. The underlying misunderstanding is treating "where the drop concentrates" as "what changed." The cheapest diagnostic is the reweighting check shown above: hold the segment mix at its baseline share and see how much of the aggregate move survives.

Stopping at the first plausible story. The symptom is a team that accepts an explanation the moment it sounds right, rather than the moment the arithmetic reconciles. The underlying misunderstanding is satisficing under time pressure. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask what percentage of the observed gap the leading hypothesis explains, computed explicitly, before presenting it.

Only looking where the dashboard already looks. The symptom is RCA confined to the filters that already exist — city, device, channel — when the actual driver is something nobody built a column for, such as a single vendor's catalogue going out of stock. The underlying misunderstanding is assuming the dashboard's dimensions are exhaustive. The cheapest diagnostic is to pull a random sample of raw sessions from the affected segment and read them, or the associated support tickets, rather than only querying pre-aggregated tables.

Reading a single time series as causal proof. The symptom is concluding that because a metric fell right after a product change, the change caused the fall. The underlying misunderstanding is ignoring everything else that happened at the same time, from a competitor's promotion to a public holiday. The cheapest diagnostic is checking whether a comparable, unaffected cohort or market moved the same way over the same window; if it did, the cause is likely external, not the change under suspicion.

8. What good looks like

Devika's team confirmed the drop was real, decomposed it to the checkout stage, segmented by city tier, and reconciled the arithmetic to within half a percentage point — the mix shift explained the great majority of the fall, with a small residual left over even after accounting for Tier-2's growing share. Rather than stop there, they pulled a sample of two hundred Tier-2 sessions that reached cart but not order, and cross-referenced them against store-level inventory logs. Sixty percent of those abandoned carts had at least one line item go out of stock at checkout during that week, concentrated in eleven of Mashaal's forty-one Tier-2 dark stores that had opened in the previous three weeks and were still stabilising their stock levels. That residual, not the discount programme anyone had first suspected, was the addressable cause. The team proposed holding the twelve-store expansion decision for two weeks, not indefinitely, while the eleven affected stores' inventory stabilised, and re-measuring Tier-2 conversion on a cohort basis rather than a cross-sectional one to see whether it converged toward the Tier-1 rate as those stores matured.

9. Closing

Devika walked into the 13 March meeting with three findings, not one story: conversion fell mainly because Tier-2 volume grew and Tier-2 has always converted lower than Tier-1; a residual within that gap traced to inventory instability at eleven specific stores rather than to the discount programme, which the board had been ready to blame; and cohort data suggested the gap narrows as stores mature, which meant the correct decision was a two-week hold and a targeted inventory fix, not a wholesale rollback of Tier-2 expansion or of the pricing strategy. The board approved the hold, deferred the twelve-store vote by two weeks, and asked for the cohort-maturation view as a standing slide in future reviews. What Devika's team should study next follows directly from what this analysis could and could not settle: signal versus noise, to know how much random variation to expect before treating any future dip as worth investigating at all, and decomposing retention changes, since the same reconciliation logic applies once a metric compounds over multiple weeks rather than appearing in a single snapshot. Two questions worth sitting with: when a root cause analysis and a controlled experiment disagree about what caused a metric to move, which should a manager trust, and why; and how would you know, without segmenting further, that you had segmented enough to trust the number in front of you?

Padav: one point one four

Lens for this case: root cause analysis of a metric change. Search-to-booking conversion fell 1.14 percentage points in eleven weeks. Six people have found the cause, and no two of them agree.

1. Sunday night, Baner

On Sunday, 8 March 2026, at half past eleven at night, Meghna Sarkar was in her flat in Baner, Pune, with a spreadsheet open on one screen and, on the other, a slide she had rebuilt four times. The slide had a single line chart on it. The line started at 6.39 percent in the week ending 21 December and finished at 5.25 percent in the week ending that evening. Holi had been on Wednesday; the buses had been full; the line had not moved.

Meghna was Director of Product for Demand at Padav. At ten o'clock on Monday morning she had to present to the leadership team, and on Wednesday 11 March the board would meet to approve the summer capacity plan and a ₹40 crore marketing commitment for April to June. Between now and then she was expected to say what had caused the drop and what Padav would do about it.

At 1.14 percentage points off a base of 6.39, the fall was eighteen percent of the company's conversion rate. On the current run rate it was worth about ₹58 crore of annual revenue. Six colleagues had told her, in the past three weeks, what had caused it. Each of them had brought evidence. She had been unable to make any two pieces of that evidence sit in the same table.

2. Company history

Padav Travel Technologies was founded in Pune in 2017 by Arunabh Ghosh and Joel Fernandes, who had spent their twenties selling inventory software to private bus operators in Maharashtra and Telangana. The insight was mundane and correct: India's inter-city bus market ran on four lakh privately owned coaches and on phone calls to travel agents, and the operators had no way to fill the last eleven seats.

By March 2026 Padav was the second or third largest online seller of inter-city bus seats in India, depending on whose numbers one used. It listed about 2,900 operators, sold roughly 8.5 lakh seats in an ordinary week and 11 lakh in a festival week, took a commission of eight to ten percent plus a convenience fee, and ran a second business — Padav Manager — selling inventory, dynamic pricing and GPS tracking software to 1,240 of those operators at ₹9,000 to ₹65,000 a month. Weekly gross booking value in a normal week was about ₹49 crore. The company had raised ₹730 crore and had been profitable at the contribution line since 2024.

One decision from 2022 still governed what Padav could do. In the summer of that year, fighting for inventory in the south, Joel had signed an exclusive distribution agreement with the Vindhya Group, a family-owned operator with 1,900 coaches across Karnataka, Telangana and Tamil Nadu. Vindhya guaranteed Padav first call on seat allocation on 61 high-demand corridors; Padav guaranteed Vindhya a most-favoured-nation clause on the convenience fee, meaning Padav could not charge a customer less on any competing operator's ticket than it charged on Vindhya's. The agreement had won Padav the south. It also meant that in 2026 the company could not discount its way out of a conversion problem on a single route without repricing the whole book. The agreement came up for renewal on 31 March 2026.

A second decision, smaller at the time, mattered more than anyone expected. In 2023, to cut cost and to prepare for the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, Vaishnavi Iyengar migrated Padav off a commercial analytics suite onto a self-hosted event pipeline. It saved ₹4.2 crore a year and gave the company full control of personal data. It also meant Padav had no session replay, no vendor to call at midnight, and a client-side event schema maintained by three people across two time zones.

3. The industry

Online bus ticketing in India in 2026 was a business of thin margins and hard peaks. redBus, part of the MakeMyTrip group, was the category leader and the reference point for every conversation Padav's board had. AbhiBus, Paytm and PhonePe sold tickets inside larger apps. State transport corporations sold directly through their own portals, and IRCTC sat beside all of it as the default for anyone whose journey could be made by train. The ONDC network had begun listing mobility sellers, which promised to commoditise discovery in a way that nobody at Padav had yet modelled.

Three macro forces bore on the January and February numbers. Diesel prices had risen through the winter, and operators had passed through fare increases averaging seven percent since November, which raised the average ticket from ₹645 to ₹690 and made the convenience fee a more visible fraction of the total. New expressway capacity — the Samruddhi Mahamarg corridor in Maharashtra chief among it — had cut journey times and encouraged operators to add departures. And Vande Bharat services had been extended on three corridors that together accounted for eleven percent of Padav's volume, offering a four-hour daylight alternative to an eight-hour overnight bus at a comparable fare.

Padav's exposure beyond India was modest and profitable. Ravi Subramanian's team in New Jersey sold a white-label booking API to overseas travel retailers serving the Indian diaspora. The largest was Sarab Travel LLC in Dubai, which sold India bus and rail tickets to GCC-based travellers and contributed ₹27 crore of annual gross booking value at a higher take rate than the consumer app. Sarab's contract was up for renewal on 15 March.

4. The situation in detail

On 22 December, Padav shipped version 8.0 of its Android and iOS apps. The centrepiece was a rebuilt search-results page designed by Tobias Ritter's team in Berlin: instead of the default sort by departure time, results were ranked by a composite "Padav Score" combining price, operator rating, on-time history and seat availability. The team had shipped it with a two percent holdout, which was the standard practice, and had moved on to the summer roadmap.

On 1 January the DPDP consent revision went live. Users saw a consent screen on first open after upgrade; analytics events classified as non-essential were withheld unless consent was given. Thirty-four percent of users declined. This was expected, was discussed in the release note, and was described there as having "no material effect on reporting, since core funnel events are server-side".

On 6 January, Yamini Kulkarni's platform team in Bengaluru upgraded the wrapper around Padav's payment integration. The change improved cold-start time by 340 milliseconds on low-end devices. In the same commit, a client-side retry that had silently re-attempted failed UPI intent handoffs was removed, on the ground that the payment aggregator had introduced its own retry and the duplicate was causing double-charge tickets. The removal was tested on the team's own devices, all running Android 13 or later.

On 14 and 15 January, Sankranti and Pongal produced the largest booking week in Padav's history: 9.72 lakh seats and ₹70.9 crore of gross booking value. Nobody looked at the conversion rate that week, because nobody looks at ratios during a peak.

The alert fired on 29 January, when the four-week trailing conversion rate crossed below 5.6 percent. The first explanation offered, by Arunabh, was the redesign: it was the biggest change, it had shipped closest to the start of the decline, and it had changed the first screen every user sees.

Tobias contested it and produced the holdout on 9 February. Users held out of the new search page converted at 5.71 percent against 5.47 percent for the treated group in the same week — a real but small difference of 0.24 points, a fifth of the observed drop. Arunabh accepted the number reluctantly. It was ten days before anyone noticed that the holdout had been configured for iOS and Android 12-and-above only, because the experiment framework's older Android client had a known sampling bug that the team had deprioritised in November.

Vaishnavi's team in Toronto came at it differently. On 12 February she circulated a note arguing that part of the fall was not real at all: the consent change had reduced client-side event capture, and any funnel metric computed from client events would move for that reason alone. The note was persuasive, and it bought the company two weeks of calm. What it did not say — because Vaishnavi did not establish it until the following Friday — was that the two ends of Padav's conversion ratio were logged differently. The denominator, search_performed, was a client event and therefore consent-gated. The numerator, booking_confirmed, was written server-side at ticket issuance and was not gated at all. A consent change that suppresses searches but not bookings raises measured conversion. Whatever the consent gating had done, it had not made the line go down.

Joel's explanation arrived on 20 February, and it came with a contract. On 27 January a route-level carve-out he had agreed with Vindhya in November had taken effect, permitting Vindhya to hold back up to twenty percent of seats on named corridors for its own direct channel. On four of Padav's top ten corridors, available seats fell between twelve and twenty-four percent. Fewer seats means more sold-out searches, and a sold-out search converts at zero.

Priyanka Rane's customer-experience team in Singapore reported a forty-one percent rise in tickets tagged "booking failed / amount debited" between December and February. Her team had, separately, revised the refund SLA messaging on 8 January and recut the complaint taxonomy at the same time, so the December and February tags did not mean quite the same thing.

And on 2 March, an analyst on Meghna's own team produced the table that unsettled everything: conversion cut by device and by user type, in which almost every cell was flat and the aggregate had still fallen.

5. The people

Meghna Sarkar, Director of Product, Demand, Pune. Owns Monday's presentation. Her stated position is that the company has not yet decomposed the metric and should not act until it has. Her incentive is a summer plan she has already staffed. What she is not saying is that her own team's performance-marketing budget rose from ₹4.1 crore to ₹7.3 crore in January, which brought a large cohort of first-time users whose conversion has always been a third of a returning user's.

Arunabh Ghosh, co-founder and CEO, Pune. Position: roll back the search redesign and stop the bleeding before the summer. Incentive: the Vindhya renewal on 31 March, which he negotiated in 2022 and regards as the company's principal asset. What he is not saying is that Vindhya has already given informal notice on two of four regions, and that a conversion story blamed on the app is a story that does not raise questions about inventory.

Yamini Kulkarni, VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Position: the problem is the Android long tail and the checkout, and she wants a four-month platform rebuild funded in the summer plan. Incentive: that budget. What she is not saying, and what appears only in a commit message from 6 January, is that her team removed the client-side payment retry and never tested the change on Android 11 or below, which is 31 percent of Padav's traffic and 44 percent of its tier-3 traffic.

Tobias Ritter, Design Director, Berlin. Position: the redesign has been scapegoated and the holdout proves it; the ranking change improved operator discovery and should stay. Incentive: his team's standing after two years of arguing for design's autonomy. What he is not saying is that he knew of the experiment framework's Android sampling bug in November and agreed to defer the fix.

Vaishnavi Iyengar, Head of Data, Toronto. Position: measurement first — freeze conclusions for two weeks and rebuild funnel events with server-side parity. Incentive: the credibility of the 2023 pipeline migration she led and defends annually at budget time. What she is not saying, as of Sunday night, is the direction of the consent bias: her 12 February note implied the drop might be an artefact, and by 27 February she knew that if anything the artefact runs the other way and the true fall is larger than 1.14 points.

Joel Fernandes, co-founder and Head of Supply, Hyderabad. Position: this is an inventory problem; win the seats back and conversion returns. Incentive: a renewal bonus tied to Vindhya signing by 31 March. What he is not saying is that the November carve-out was his concession, made to secure the renewal, and that it was not brought to the product team at all.

Priyanka Rane, Head of Customer Experience, Singapore. Position: trust is the cause — customers who lost money on a failed booking in January are not coming back, and word travels in a market where a bus ticket is a household decision. Incentive: a CSAT target and a headcount request. What she is not saying is that her January taxonomy change makes the forty-one percent rise partly an artefact of her own reclassification, which her deputy flagged in an internal note she has not circulated.

Exhibit 3 is Yamini's evidence and it is the cleanest break in the case: a 7.3 point fall in payment success on Android 11 and below, beginning in the week that contains the 6 January SDK upgrade, with iOS and modern Android unmoved. On 31 percent of traffic, a 7.3 point fall in the last step of the funnel is worth roughly 0.22 points of overall conversion — real, serious, and about a fifth of the problem. It is also the exhibit whose exclusion footnote matters most: the share of orders with no device band doubled over the period, and nobody knows which band those orders belong to.

Exhibit 4. Padav-recorded bookings versus operator-reported seats issued, four weeks

Operator-reported seats are the sum of the daily manifest files returned by operator inventory systems, received with a lag of up to 48 hours and reconciled monthly. From 1 February, the Vindhya Group began reporting seats sold through its own direct channel within the same PNR series it uses for Padav; the reconciliation logic has not been updated for this. Eleven smaller operators, together about 4 percent of volume, do not return manifests at all and are imputed from the previous month's ratio.

Exhibit 4 was produced by finance to test whether Padav was losing bookings or losing count of them, and it has been used in two meetings to argue that the drop is a reporting artefact — look, the operators say we sold more than we recorded. The footnote disposes of that: the variance appears in precisely the week that Vindhya's reporting changed, and the change is of the kind that would create exactly this variance whether or not Padav's own counts were correct. Exhibit 4 and Exhibit 1 cannot both be taken at face value, and the case for taking either is weak.

Exhibit 5. Analytics consent and event capture, January to February 2026

Compiled by the data platform team, 27 February 2026. No baseline exists for December because consent was not collected before 1 January. booking_confirmed is written server-side at ticket issuance and is classified as essential processing, so it is not subject to consent. search_performed is a client event classified as non-essential. Version 7.x users, 21 percent of February sessions, had not yet been prompted for consent. Capture rates are measured against server access logs for the search endpoint.

Exhibit 5 is the exhibit that most changes the shape of the problem and it is the one nobody in the company has yet read carefully. If only 79 percent of searches are captured but 100 percent of bookings are, then the conversion ratio in Exhibit 1 has a systematically understated denominator from January onwards — which means the reported 5.25 percent is too high, not too low, and the true decline is larger than 1.14 points. The exhibit also has no December baseline, so the size of the correction cannot be computed from it. Applied crudely, a denominator understated by 21 percent would put February's true conversion nearer 4.2 percent, which is not a conversion problem but a different company.

Exhibit 6 is Joel's exhibit, and it makes and unmakes his case in the same picture. On the four carve-out corridors, seats fell 14 to 24 percent and conversion fell 15 to 19 percent — as tight a correspondence as anyone could want. But conversion also fell 10 to 21 percent on the six corridors where supply rose, including Mumbai–Nagpur, where supply rose 11 percent and conversion fell 21 percent, and where a new Vande Bharat service and the expressway have both changed the corridor since December. Whatever is happening is happening everywhere; the carve-out may be adding to it on four routes.

7. Voices

"We changed the first screen of the app on 22 December and the number started falling on 4 January. I do not need a regression to read that. Put the old sort back for the summer, and we can be clever again in August."

Arunabh Ghosh, in the Monday leadership review, 2 March

"The holdout says 0.24 points. I will say it again in whatever meeting you like. If the number were the redesign, the held-out users would be sitting at 6.4 percent, and they are not, they are at 5.71."

Tobias Ritter, Berlin, in the #search channel, 9 February

"Tobias — the holdout ran on iOS and Android 12+. It has never contained a single Android 10 device. I raised the sampling bug in November. I am not saying the redesign is the cause. I am saying the holdout cannot tell us."

Vaishnavi Iyengar, Toronto, reply in the same thread, 19 February, 11.42 p.m. EST

"My agents in Singapore are taking the 6 a.m. India calls. Four weeks running, the same sentence: 'paisa cut gaya, ticket nahin aaya.' I do not know what your dashboards say. I know what the queue sounds like at seven in the morning."

Priyanka Rane, Singapore, e-mail to Meghna Sarkar, 24 February

"On Bengaluru–Hyderabad we had 41,000 seats a week in December and we have 31,000 now. Every search that returns 'sold out' is a search that converts at zero. You are looking for a bug. I am telling you the shelf is empty."

Joel Fernandes, Hyderabad, in the supply review, 20 February

"Sarab's conversion is down 16 percent too, and they are on our API, not our app. That should settle the design argument."

Ravi Subramanian, New Jersey, on the global call, 2 March

"Meghna — before Monday, please note that search_performed is gated and booking_confirmed is not. I have been turning this over since Friday. I think our measured conversion is flattered, not depressed, by the consent change. I would like to be wrong."

Vaishnavi Iyengar, Toronto, direct message to Meghna Sarkar, Saturday 7 March, 9.14 p.m. IST

8. The options as Meghna currently sees them

Option A — roll back the search ranking. Restore the departure-time default for the summer, keep the Padav Score as an optional sort. It is two days of work, it satisfies the CEO, and the holdout says it is worth 0.24 points at best. It also throws away the one clean experiment the company ran, and it tells Tobias's team that evidence loses to seniority.

Option B — emergency fix on checkout. Restore the client-side retry behind a device check, add a fallback for UPI intent handoff failures on older Android, and ship inside ten days before the code freeze on 20 March. Exhibit 3 supports it; it is worth perhaps 0.22 points; and Yamini will attach a four-month platform rebuild to the request.

Option C — fight for inventory. Reopen the Vindhya carve-out before the 31 March renewal, and buy supply on the four affected corridors by funding operator incentives — constrained by the most-favoured-nation clause, which turns a corridor-level concession into a book-wide one. Joel supports it; Arunabh will resist anything that reopens the agreement three weeks before renewal.

Option D — declare the measurement broken and fix it first. Two weeks, server-side funnel parity, a proper December baseline reconstructed from access logs, and a board told that the company does not yet know. It is the only option that addresses Exhibit 5, and it is the only one that arrives at the board with no plan attached.

Each of the four names a cause and offers a remedy sized to it. The sizes are the difficulty: 0.24 points, 0.22 points, something under 0.3 points on four corridors, and a measurement correction of unknown sign and possibly large magnitude. They do not add to 1.14, and two of them cannot be added at all because the populations overlap. Nobody in the company has yet proposed the fifth option, which is that the January marketing spend bought 5 percentage points of new-user share and that a third of the fall is the price of growth working exactly as designed — an explanation that would require Meghna to open with her own budget rather than someone else's bug.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The leadership review is at 10 a.m. on Monday 9 March. The board meets on Wednesday 11 March to approve the summer plan, including ₹40 crore of marketing for April to June, and a promised ESOP liquidity event for 340 employees whose pricing was indicated against a March run rate. Engineering enters code freeze on 20 March and does not ship again until 5 June, because the April-to-June peak carries 38 percent of annual volume. The Vindhya agreement renews or lapses on 31 March, and the most-favoured-nation clause means any convenience-fee concession on one corridor applies to the whole book, worth roughly ₹31 crore a year. The Sarab contract in Dubai renews on 15 March. The DPDP consent architecture cannot be relaxed; only the classification of individual events can be revisited, and Padav's external counsel has asked for two weeks' notice on any such change. Vaishnavi has four analysts and two of them are on the pipeline migration's final cutover. And the experiment framework's Android sampling bug is fixed in a branch that has not been merged since November.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1 alone, state precisely what changed: which step of the funnel, over which weeks, and by how much. What does Exhibit 1 not let you say?

2. Exhibit 2's aggregate is 5.59 percent and Exhibit 1's is 5.26 percent for the same period. Explain the gap. Which of the two should appear on the board slide, and what would you have to write underneath it?

3. Decompose the 1.06-point fall between December and late February into mix, rate and measurement. Show which components you can size from the case, which you can bound, and which you cannot touch.

4. Exhibit 6 shows conversion falling on corridors where supply rose. Design the cut of the data that would distinguish Joel's inventory explanation from a cause that is common to all corridors. What would each result look like?

5. Vaishnavi's message on Saturday night implies the true fall is larger than reported. If she is right, which of the four options changes, and which stakeholder's position becomes untenable? If she is wrong, what has the company lost by waiting two weeks to find out?

6. What should Meghna do on Monday morning, in the order she should do it — and what exactly should she say to the board on Wednesday, given that ₹40 crore of summer marketing, a supplier renewal and 340 employees' liquidity all depend on a number she cannot yet explain?

Sunday, twenty past midnight

Meghna had drawn a fishbone on the back of an envelope at about eleven, with six ribs, and had crossed out two of them, and had then drawn arrows between three of the remaining four, because a customer on an Android 10 phone whose payment failed in January would also be a customer who searched less in February and would appear in Exhibit 2 as a mix change. The causes were not in separate bones. They were in each other.

On the second screen, Vaishnavi's message was still open. I would like to be wrong. Meghna typed a reply, deleted it, and typed a different one, and did not send that either. Outside, the last of the night buses were pulling out of the Wakad stop on the Mumbai highway, full, on time, and counted twice.
